rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate the elution window and identify critical pairs, with a strong final solvent to minimize the risk of missing compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.

Raise temperature while keeping the gradient fixed to test selectivity around the single unresolved pair. The current elution window leaves ample margin below 10 minutes, so prioritize improving that pair without sacrificing its neighbors.
The central peak pattern suggests an elution-order crossover as temperature rises. Test 55 C with a shallower gradient to separate that cluster while aiming to keep the last peak within 10 minutes.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method. Keep temperature and solvent endpoints fixed to isolate the effect on the marginally resolved pair.
Shorten the gradient another two minutes to test the speed limit at 55 C. Watch both central critical pairs: the previous shortening improved one slightly but reduced the other's resolution.

Retain injection 4 as the fastest fully resolved method so far, and explore the low-temperature selectivity branch with a shorter gradient. Cooling may separate the central cluster in a different elution order, opening a faster route to full resolution.

Test a faster, high-temperature branch where the currently limiting pair may reverse elution order and regain separation. Injection 4 remains the fully resolved fallback while this run probes whether a substantially shorter method is feasible.

Shorten the 60 C gradient one step to test whether the reversed central pair gains separation as the gradient steepens. Monitor its neighboring pair, which had only moderate resolution at eight minutes.

Test a higher starting organic fraction to advance elution while making the gradient slope shallower than injection 5. This may recover the limiting central pair’s resolution at a shorter runtime than injection 4; also check for compression of the early peaks.

Lower the starting organic fraction to test the opposite selectivity shift from injection 9, where the central pair collapsed. This may restore full resolution at a shorter elution time than injection 4, though the other central pair must also remain above 1.5.

Test whether a modest increase in starting organic strengthens the reversed central pair seen in injection 7 while preserving its neighbors. This explores a substantially faster route to full resolution, with injection 10 retained as the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Test whether a shallower gradient resolves the central cluster at 40 C, establishing an alternative selectivity window for subsequent acceleration. The last peak is expected near 10 minutes, so this is an information-gathering run rather than a likely speed improvement.

Probe 35 C for an alternative central-cluster selectivity window between the crowded 25 C result and the nearly resolved 40 C result. Keep the original gradient fixed to isolate temperature effects, retaining injection 10 as the fastest fully resolved fallback.
Shorten the fastest fully resolved method by one grid step to establish its speed boundary. Both central pairs were close to R = 1.5 in injection 10, so retain that method if either loses resolution.

Probe an intermediate-temperature, steep-gradient branch for a different central-cluster elution pattern that could support a much faster separation. Injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed method with the maximum CRF.

Refine the fully resolved 40 C branch using a higher starting organic fraction and a shorter gradient to advance the last peak. This tests whether its central-pair resolution can be preserved while removing the time penalty seen in injection 12.

Use the final organic fraction to tune the slope between injections 4 and 5, targeting just enough separation for the limiting central pair. This may match full resolution at a slightly shorter elution time than injection 10.

Lower the endpoint one more grid step to recover the small resolution deficit in injection 17. This should provide a fully resolved alternative near eight minutes with more balanced central-pair margins than injection 10.

Test whether 50 C balances the central pairs at a higher starting organic fraction, while the longer gradient restores separation lost in injection 9. This could approach injection 10’s speed with improved resolution margins; monitor the early pair for compression.

Set the slope between injections 17 and 18 to target full resolution with less excess separation and a shorter programmed gradient. The strong final solvent should still allow all compounds to elute comfortably within 10 minutes.

Refine the 40 C branch by increasing starting organic, which also makes the gradient shallower at fixed duration. This tests whether the central pair can reach full resolution while advancing the last peak; watch the early pair for compression.

Preserve injection 10’s successful starting composition, slope, and temperature while shortening the programmed gradient and lowering its endpoint. All peaks previously eluted before this new gradient ends, so the separation should remain fully resolved.

Increase the endpoint one grid step from injection 22 to test a modest acceleration between the fully resolved and under-resolved slopes already observed. Retain injection 22 if the central pair drops below R = 1.5.

Back off to the fully resolving slope of injection 22 while shortening the programmed gradient to eight minutes. Because the last peak previously eluted at 7.60 minutes, this lower endpoint should preserve the maximum CRF without prolonging elution.

Use the final injection to seek more balanced resolution margins by pairing a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient at 55 C. Injection 24 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method, already achieving the maximum CRF.
